A D J O U R N M E N T I N
A THERLEY TRIAL.

When the Court assembled this morning in preparation for the continued hearing of the Atherley case, His Lordship addressed the jury and said he regretted having to inform them that their foreman Mr. P. M. N. da Silva, was very ill and it was impossible for him to sit through the day's hearing.
As the case could not go on without him, His Lordship thought the best thing to do would be to adjourn for the day. Mr. Silva was hoping, he understood, to be in a fit condition to sit to-morrow.
The case was adjourned until to-morrow morning, at 10.30.
A Chinese constable was changed before Mr. R. E. LindseLL at the Central Magistracy this morning with larceny and alternatively with receiving stolen property.

At the previous hearing, the complainant, Mr. William Allen, said that he lost an overcont, a gold watch and a chain, and a sum of money, while on his way home from a dinner. The missing articles, including $22 in bank notes, were found by Detective Sergeant O'Donovan in a room occupied by the defendant at Queen's Road East.

In a long statement the defendant said that he met an old friend whom he invited to his cubicle that night. They had some Chinese wine together and the friend got drunk. Later the visitor went away, leaving the overcoat and a watch and chain in defendant's charge. Defendant called his wife as a witness, and certain portions of his statement were borne out by the woman. Mr. W. R. Scott (A.S.P.) said that the defendant had served for eleven months and had a good record.
The Magistrate held that there was not sufficient evidence to conflict on the charge of larceny. He convicted on the charge of receiving stolen property, the sentence being six months' hard labour.

Repairs which the s.s. "Empress of Asia" is undergoing at Woo-sung as a consequence of the collision with the s.s. "Tungshing" will probably be completed in time for the vessel to leave that port on Friday.

The ship is reported to be absolutely seaworthy and it is hoped that three days' delay in schedule is all that will be necessitated. The "Empress of Asia" is due to leave Yokohama according to present arrangements, on Tuesday of next week.

Mr. Eric Rice, the Assistant Secretary to the Overseas League arrived in the Colony yesterday, January 12, and is staying at the Hongkong Hotel. He is anxious to meet members of the League during his fortnight's visit to the Colony, and would be glad to hear from anyone interested in the activities of the League.

Summoned at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning for leaving his motor car unattended in Nathan Road, Mr. E. C. Bell was severely rebuked by the Magistrate (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) and warned of the consequences of treating the Court with disrespect. This observation was made as the defendant had disregarded the summons to attend yesterday and also scorned the evidence of an Indian constable this morning.

Applying under that section of the Ordinance which permits a landlord if he makes improvements in a house to the extent of $500, to charge extra in the rent, the Chinese landlord of No. 9, Lower Laschar Row sought at the Summary Court this morning to increase the rent of the lessee; 8 per cent. of $918 yearly.

R. A. Wadeson (for the plaintiff) and Mr. D. McCallum, Mr. Wadeson emphasising the nature of the alterations to the house, consisting of replacing floors, new joints, floor bonds tile coverings, dividing living rooms on three floors into kitchen and living room by erecting brick wall, etc. This he claimed constituted ground for an increase in the rateable value.
Mr. McCallum held, however, and His Lordship agreed with him that a large percentage of the work was for necessary repairs, and not improvements in respect of which the Ordinance applied.
His Lordship went into the accounts in detail and finding that $198 only had been spent on actual improvements he gave judgment for the tenant.

An order was made by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning for confiscation of 35 taels of opium found on board the s.a. "Tenyo Maru." The evidence of an Indian guard was that he found the opium wrapped in a coat and dumped in the lavatory.

On a charge of unlawful possession of 18 taels of opium, a Chinese was fined $2,000 or eight months' hard labour in default. The opium was found concealed under the clothing when the man was searched at the Wing Lok wharf on his way from Macao.
PANTRY BOY. AND A MOTOR CAR.

An amended charge of negligently damaging a tram car was preferred, this morning against the pantry boy who was before the Central Magistrate yesterday on a charge of driving a motor car without a licence.
After new evidence it was found that the defendant had wilfully turned the switch on and worked the self-starter.

Defendant was fined $10, or fourteen days, and no order was made for compensation to the Tramway Company, as His Worship was informed that Mr. Harry Kong, the owner of the motor car, had already paid $25.

Interesting developments are expected to follow two seizures effected by the authorities, of contraband, in different parts of the Colony.

A long search on the s.s. "Benavón" yesterday, after her arrival from Europe via Singapore, brought forth about 53 revolvers and 5,000 rounds of ammunition. At a conservative estimate this lot would fetch several thousands of dollars should they have reached their destination.
Chief Preventive Officer S. J. Clarke, Revenue Officers Ward and Beattie were in charge. As far as is known the arms were discovered in the firemen's quarters and a number of arrests were made.

On Monday night Police detectives visited a Chinese house in Tai Wong Street West (Wanchai) where they found three "bombs." Details have not been given but it may be that the containers had some kind of explosive and were not bombs in the understood sense of the word.
The same party of Police then raided a house in Lok Hing Lane, close to Central Station, where a revolver and two other firearms were found, together with ammunition.
Arrests were also made by the Police in their case.

A Chinese youth was fined $10, or fourteen days' hard labour, and he was further asked to furnish a bond in a surety of $50 to be of good behaviour, when he was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with disorderly conduct at a Chinese tea-house.

Evidence was given that the defendant had a dispute with a waitress and had to be turned out. He came later with a hatchet and threatened to do harm to the inmates. The master of the teahouse blew a police whistle and the youth was arrested.

Although the newspaper despatches from Washington claim that the Government is rather concerned over the Mexican attitude regarding the new Mexican land laws, a statement issued in Washington to-day declares that President Coolidge is still convinced that the Mexican Government will find a way to fulfill its obligations regarding the protection of Americans in connection with the new land and petroleum legislation.

President Coolidge recognises Mexico's right to legislate in her domestic affairs as she sees fit, but it is pointed out that the Washington Government could not fail to take cognizance of any aspect of Mexican laws retroactively affecting American interests in Mexico.

A remarkable "lost and found" incident regarding a $900 diamond bracelet was brought to a close thls morning when this costly article was returned by the Police to its rightful owner through a local resident who picked it up.
Mr. Harry Fong, the Chinese dentist who has been in Hongkong for many years, was the finder and the Chinese lady who owned the bracelet gave him appropriate recognition.
Several days ago the lady reported to the Police that her bracelet was missing. Mr. Fong found it, handed it in at Central Station and the bracelet was restored.
The National Automobile Chamber of Commerce has authorised an appropriation of ten million dollars "to assure the public and motor manufacturers of an adequate supply of rubber at reasonable prices."
A Committee has been appointed to organise the work. It will apply for a charter. Several of the largest companies have announced their readiness to take allotment of stock.

Mr. Reeves, the General Manager of the Chamber, stated that it was likely that small producers of rubber in the far corners of the world who were not held by the British "monopoly" would sell their rubber if they were assured of a centralised shipping point where the material could be pooled.

The provisional estimates for 1925 show a tremendous increase in native rubber production of 50 per cent. since 1924, giving a total of 129,700 tons gross or 84,000 net compared with 104,000 tons of estate rubber, which increased only 15 per cent.

Washington, Jan. 12.
Major-General William Lassiter has been appointed to succeed General Pershing as Head of the Tacna-Arica Plebiscite Commission.
Major-General Lassiter, who is at present in Panama, has been instructed to proceed to Arica forthwith to enable General Pershing to return to the United States for medical treatment.
NO ROYAL ROAD TO ITS RECOVERY

A demand for the restoration of the eight-hour day in mines was the chief point in the evidence submitted to the Coal Commission on behalf of the owners, who declared that the standards of living must rest on a stable and economic conditions, whilst savings could also be effected and earnings could be increased if the miners attended their work with greater regularity. It was pointed out that absenteeism in Scotland averages 3½ per cent. in England and Wales 8¼ per cent.

The owners expressed their willingness to meet the miners with the utmost goodwill, but they were opposed to the establishment of compulsory machinery for the settlement of disputes. They were unable to point to any royal road for the recovery of the industry, but were confident that lower costs of production would stimulate an already growing demand for British coal.

Mr. Evan Williams, President of the Mining Association of Great Britain, questioned by the Chairman, Sir Herbert Samuel, declared that they were not afraid of the competition of oil in the future. He believed that in the case of big liners the cost of oil burning was greatly in excess of coal burning. There was no reason why in the course of time coal should not be put in liners in a form enabling them to use it with greater economy than oil.

He expressed the opinion that the very existence of Great Britain depended upon a larger export trade in coal. Large contracts were often lost, simply through a difference of  $ 1\frac{1}{2}d $, or 3d. per ton in price.
The Chairman declared that if the Mining Association's proposals were accepted the British miners would be working longer than French, Belgian, and German miners.

Mr. Evan Williams replied that their wages would be considerably higher. He asserted that the unrest in the industry was not spontaneous, but was the result of a deliberate attempt by the miners' leaders to prevent the reconstruction of the industry by private enterprise after decontrol.

A memorandum from the Mining Association, which was submitted prior to the taking of evidence, said that if the railway wages bill were reduced all rates for mineral goods traffic could be reduced by 25 per cent.

The conference between the employers and the representatives of the strikers in the anthracite coal mines was adjourned without a settlement and without a date for the renewal of the negotiations being determined.
The mine owners insisted upon complete arbitration, whilst the miners maintained that arbitration was only acceptable on the basis of increased wages without any reductions.

It is announced from Wilkes-barre (Pennsylvania) that the Grievance Committee of the Pennsylvania Coal Company today decided to launch a movement to call out all anthracite mine maintenance men for the purpose of forcing the issue and it is generally believed there that the strikers will make a determined effort to tie up the mines completely.
